section.title: Understand the incentives behind a performance plan
section.deck: Ethan Evans explains how a target can force neglected performance conversations while also biasing managers toward departure.

blocks.question: What do you think of stack ranking, attrition targets, and performance improvement plans?
answer: Evans describes an Amazon attrition-target system from his management experience: a list of people whose departure was considered unregretted, with pressure to reach an annual proportion through improvement, resignation, or termination. His quoted percentages vary by period and are historical recollections, not verified current policy.

He says that when Amazon experimentally removed the target, managers stopped having difficult conversations with struggling performers, and the goal returned. Managers may avoid acting when a person is well liked, especially in a large organization where the immediate cost is not obvious to them. The target forced attention to a real problem.

The other side is distortion. A quota can put someone on a list who still had a plausible chance of success. Once a manager has mentally decided a person should leave, confirmation bias can make the improvement plan psychologically unrealistic. Evans believes many plans therefore function more as a route to departure than an open-minded attempt to improve.

He reports unsuccessful experiences coaching roughly half a dozen people on Amazon PIPs and similar outcomes among people who did not use his coaching. He now urges people in that situation to prepare for another job rather than rely on reversal. That is a strong warning based on his cases, not a measured universal failure rate.

Even a manager starting with good intentions may face pressure from HR and leadership to count an exit, or to name another person if the first improves. Evans’s broader diagnosis is that companies often fail to train managers for early, useful performance conversations, then depend on a distorted late-stage process.
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: What prevents a manager from presenting an employee unfairly to HR?
answer: Evans distinguishes removing one employee from repeatedly driving people out. A pattern of high turnover can eventually expose a manager, but one case may remain difficult to challenge. The manager usually has higher status and can frame the issue for HR before the employee realizes that a dispute is developing.

He illustrates narrative ambiguity with code reviews. The same large number of reviews can be described as improving everyone’s code and developing the team, or as nitpicking others while contributing little original implementation. Counts do not by themselves determine which interpretation is accurate.

He says he has not personally used this power to target someone unfairly, and notes that keeping capable partners serves a manager’s goals. His concern is the vulnerability to a vindictive manager or a genuinely different view of what constitutes useful work. HR hearing a familiar denial of poor performance may not easily distinguish a legitimate complaint.

His practical conclusion is to repair the relationship where possible or find a different manager, rather than assume HR will necessarily rescue the employee. This is his description of a power imbalance, not approval of retaliation or a claim that every organization lacks checks.
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
